Sangwu Park Wonjoong Kim Yeonjun In Chanyoung Park *
KAIST
{sangwu.park, wjkim, yeonjun.in, cy.park}@kaist.ac.kr
Abstract
Vision-language-action (VLA) models are ex-
pected to follow instructions like their language
backbones, yet prior work has focused on What-
level instructions that specify the task rather
than How-level instructions that specify how to
carry it out. Through our diagnoses, we find
that How-level instructions do not help current
VLAs and lower task success. We hypothesize
that pairing each training episode with a single
instruction limits How-level instruction follow-
ing, and show that training with segment-level
enriched instructions makes actions respond to
such instructions without consistently raising
task success. To measure How-level instruc-
tion following beyond standard benchmarks,
we introduce SIMPLER-IN, where success re-
quires conditions given only in the instruction.
It shows that the gained responsiveness does
not extend to demanding or out-of-distribution
How-level instructions. How-level instruction
following thus remains an open challenge.1
1 Introduction
Completing a task specified by a language instruc-
tion does not necessarily mean following instruc-
tions on how to perform it. For example, “put the
carrot on the plate” specifieswhata robot should
accomplish, whereas “grasp the carrot by its green
end” specifieshowto accomplish it. This distinc-
tion is particularly important for vision-language-
action (VLA) models, which generate robot ac-
tions from visual observations and language in-
structions (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024;
Black et al., 2024; Intelligence et al., 2025; Bjorck
et al., 2025). Following instructions abouthow
to act would enable VLAs to incorporate correc-
tions, refine actions, and adjust their behavior
through language, as widely practiced in large lan-
guage models (LLMs) and vision-language models

7 Conclusion
We find that current VLAs struggle to follow How-
level instructions. Enriched instructions based
on our data hypothesis make actions respond to
them without consistently raising task success. On
SIMPLER-IN, which requires How-level instruc-
tions for task success, all models fail on demand-
ing How-level instructions and do not follow OOD
ones. We hope that our diagnoses and SIMPLER-
IN help future work toward VLAs that follow How-
level instructions.
9

Limitations
Our experiments cover a single combination of
embodiment, simulator, and training data, the Wid-
owX robot in SIMPLER with BridgeData V2, on
short-horizon pick-and-place tasks. Other embod-
iments and longer tasks may behave differently,
which we leave for future work. We manually
check sampled corrections in offline correction,
and online intervention assumes imperfect VLM-
generated instructions by design. In online inter-
vention, the enriched models gain task success in
several cases under the same System 2, which in-
directly suggests that the given instructions can be
correct. Nevertheless, it remains possible that incor-
rect instructions account for part of the observed
failures. Enriched instructions change both the
temporal alignment of instructions and their How-
level content. In the short-horizon tasks, the task
is the same throughout an episode, so instructions
that change across segments naturally describe how
to carry out the task rather than what the task is.
Segment-level instructions thus tend to be How-
level, and our hypothesis treats them jointly. How-
ever, we acknowledge that our experiments do not
separate them, and leave separating their

A Details of the Diagnosis
A.1 Generation of Corrections
Failed episodes and timeline.Each model runs the
four WidowX tasks of SIMPLER with 24 episodes
each for up to 60 steps under the seeds 42, 142, and
242. For each failure, we label every step with one
of nine phases, such as approach, lift, and trans-
port, from the grasp state, the distance from the
end-effector to the object, the distance from the ob-
ject to the target, and the end-effector height. The
timeline lists each segment of consecutive steps
with the same phase, together with the step range
and the start and end values of these quantities.
Prompt design and corrections.We design the
prompt on 12 failed episodes. We compare three
timeline formats, the raw phase segments, seg-
ments without short grasps, and segments with
short ones merged, and three prompts that spec-
ify the critical point of the failure as a frame range,
a window of the video in percent, or indices of
